content: The purpose of creating microchapters is to achieve several specific goals. Additionally, microchapters facilitate the issuance of microcredits for Continuing Medical Education (CME). To standardize and automate the creation and cataloging of microchapters, the titles should follow a specific capitalization rule: only the first letter of the first word should be capitalized. For example, instead of Pericarditis Causes, the title should be written as Pericarditis causes. A navigation box template is available to assist in organizing content. This template can be found on the right-hand side under How to create an expanded navigation box. To set up a navigation box on a page, place the template at the top of the page. Replace the placeholder text type page name here with the name of the disease or chapter you are working on. However, do not replace the term PAGENAME. Save the navigation box template as Template:Type page name here. When editing or creating microchapters, certain elements should be removed or replaced. For instance, the WikiDoc Cardiology Network Infobox template should be removed. Replace the search infobox template (SI) with the appropriate template for the disease being addressed. The structure of the disease's homepage should mirror the structure of the navigation box. The structure of microchapters is divided into several sections, each with a specific focus: 1. Overview: This section provides a concise summary of the key aspects of the condition, with an emphasis on diagnosis and treatment. Content from copyleft government sites can serve as a useful guide. This section should include links to more detailed microchapters. 2. Patient Info: This section should include patient-friendly information sourced from government sites such as the NHLBI or NLM. The content should be written at an 8th-grade reading level and include a link to the relevant WikiDoc page at the top. 3. Pathophysiology: This section explains the biological mechanisms underlying the disease, including descriptions of embryological or developmental abnormalities, molecular and genetic abnormalities, and pathology images. 4. Demographics and Epidemiology: This section discusses the incidence and prevalence of the disease in both developed and developing countries. 5. Screening: This section outlines the screening procedures for the disease. It is typically not included in the navigation box. 6. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis: This section describes the progression of the disease if left untreated, potential complications, and the overall prognosis. 7. Causes: This section lists all conditions that can cause the disease, as well as associated conditions that do not directly cause it. A table should be included to organize and present this information comprehensively. 8. Complete Differential Diagnosis of the Causes (By Organ System): This section is not intended to describe what the disease causes or how to distinguish it from other disorders. Instead, it focuses on listing the differential diagnoses by organ system. 9. Differentiating the Disease from Other Disorders: This section highlights the distinguishing features of the disease compared to other conditions with similar symptoms, physical examination findings, or laboratory results. Organizing these distinguishing features in a table is recommended. 10. History and Symptoms: This section describes the symptoms typically reported by patients. It does not include physical examination findings. Symptoms should be organized by frequency. 11. Physical Examination: This section outlines the signs of the disease observed during a physical examination. Symptoms should not be included here. Findings should be organized into categories such as: Appearance of the Patient Vital Signs Skin Eyes Ear, Nose, and Throat Heart Lungs Abdomen Extremities Neurologic 12. Laboratory Tests: This section includes information about laboratory tests such as electrolytes (e.g., potassium, sodium), kidney function tests (e.g., creatinine, BUN), liver function tests (e.g., SGOT, SGPT), and complete blood count (e.g., WBC, hematocrit, hemoglobin). Imaging study results (e.g., chest X-rays, CT scans, MRIs) and pathology images are not included here; they belong in the Pathophysiology section. 13. Imaging Studies: This section is dedicated to imaging and other diagnostic studies. 14. Treatment: This section serves as a general heading and does not link to any specific content. Subsections include Medical Treatment and Surgery. 15. Medical Treatment: This subsection describes the medications used to treat the condition, including their dosages, duration of therapy, and guidance on escalating therapy or managing treatment failures. 16. Surgery: This subsection includes the indications for surgical intervention, pre-operative tests, details of the surgical procedure, and post-operative care. 17. Primary Prevention: This section describes interventions aimed at preventing the initial occurrence of the disease. 18. Secondary Prevention: This section focuses on interventions designed to prevent recurrence or a second occurrence of the disease. Finally, a useful tip for formatting content is to use a colon (:) at the beginning of a line to slightly indent the text to the right.
